items.name: Entity
items.doc: An entity handle. Properties read/write engine memory directly; using an entity after it was destroyed throws (check .alive).

members.doc: Stable unique id (assignable; keeps lookups consistent).

This entity's own flag. false hides it and everything under it (not drawn, no UI, no scripts), but setting a parent's `active` to false does not change the flags of its children: a child of a hidden Panel keeps `active` true. To ask whether an entity is really on, read `activeInHierarchy`.

true when this entity and every ancestor are active, i.e. it is really in the game. A child of a hidden Panel has `active` true and `activeInHierarchy` false. Use it to ask whether a menu is open; `ui.rectOf` and `ui.state` agree with it.
False once the entity was destroyed.
Transform view (position, rotation, scale).
Shortcut for transform.position (live view; assignable with vec2/vec3/[x,y]).
World-space position (get/set).

members.sig: get<K extends keyof Components>(name: K): Components[K] | null
members.doc: Live view of a component, or null if the entity lacks it.

members.sig: add<K extends keyof Components>(name: K, fields?: ComponentInit[K]): Components[K]
members.doc: Adds (or returns) a component and applies fields.

members.sig: set<K extends keyof Components>(name: K, fields: ComponentInit[K]): Components[K]
members.doc: Patches component fields (adds the component if missing).
Names of the components on this entity.

Destroys the entity (and children) at the end of the frame: the memory and the components stay until then (`alive` stays true), so a handle you hold keeps working for the rest of the frame. The entity is gone for lookups at once: world.find, world.findAll, world.findByTag and world.entities no longer return it and its id can be used by a new entity in the same frame (spawn a rebuilt screen with the same ids, no prefix needed). It leaves physics at once: no collisions and no raycast or overlap hits from the call on.

members.sig: setParent(parent: EntityLike, keepWorld?: boolean, index?: number): void
members.doc: Moves the entity under another one (null = top level). index is the place among the new parent's OTHER children (0 = first, up to their count; omitted = last), so it also reorders within the same parent. A parent is required for an index; a bad index throws. Layouts follow this order.
The script instance attached to this entity (constructed as soon as the entity is spawned or its scene loaded), or null. Its own fields are reachable: game.find("p").behaviour.hp.
Calls behaviour[method](...args) if it exists.

World-space axis-aligned rectangle { x, y, w, h } of this entity's 2D visual, or null. (x, y) is the minimum corner, i.e. the BOTTOM-LEFT in the +Y-up world: the same Rect convention as physics.overlapBox and debug.rect. Tilemap: its size as drawn (rows form or width x height) times tileSize, from the top-left corner at the entity position. Sprite and Shape2D: size and pivot (a circle is its bounding square, a line its stroked segment; the outline thickness of other shapes is ignored). Text: the laid-out box (approximate when headless, like ui.measureText). Scale and rotation are applied (the box around the rotated corners) and several visuals give their union. null when the entity has no world-space 2D visual: none at all, an empty Tilemap, or only screen-space ones (space: "screen"). Children are not included. Example: const map = world.find("map").bounds();
Touching ground below (2D pixels tolerance, default 2; 3D meters, default 0.05).
Entity JSON as in scene files.
Solid contact against the body in `direction` (the obstacle lies that way): isTouching(vec2(1, 0)) = wall on the right, vec2(0, 1) = ceiling. Triggers never count.
Immediately spawns `count` particles at this entity's ParticleEmitter (works with emitting = false). No-op with a warning when there is no renderer (headless).
Skeletal animation of this entity's Animator component (play, set, trigger, clips, events). Throws if the entity has no Animator; entity.get("Animator") answers null instead.
Named clips of this entity's SpriteAnimator (play, clips, on("clipEnded")). Throws if the entity has no SpriteAnimator; entity.get("SpriteAnimator") answers null instead.

Single-tile access to this entity's Tilemap component (getTile, setTile, width, height) and the cell <-> world conversion for both projections (cellAt, cellToWorld). Throws if the entity has no Tilemap; entity.get("Tilemap") answers null instead.
Playback of this entity's Video component (play, pause, stop, seek, time, duration, the "ended" event). Throws if the entity has no Video; entity.get("Video") answers null instead.

items.name: Behaviour
items.doc: Base class of gameplay scripts. Export a subclass as the default export of a module in scripts/ and attach it with the Script component. Class fields are defaults overridable from Script.props.

members.doc: The owning entity.
false skips update callbacks.

Default false. While time.scale is 0 (game.paused) the engine calls onUpdate and onLateUpdate only on behaviours whose runWhilePaused is true, with the REAL frame time as dt (time.dt is 0 then; time.unscaledDt is the real one). Set it as a class field (`runWhilePaused = true;`) on pause menus and anything else that must react while gameplay is frozen. onFixedUpdate never runs while paused. ui events and world.on listeners are delivered either way.
One-shot timer (scaled game time); cancelled automatically on destroy.
Repeating timer.

members.sig: tween(target: object, props: { [property: string]: number | string | readonly number[] | { [channel: string]: number } }, options?: TweenOptions): Tween
members.doc: Like tween(), but owned by this behaviour: when its entity is destroyed (or the scene unloads) the tween is dropped and `await this.tween(...).finished` never resumes, so the code after it does not run and needs no alive check. Example: await this.tween(this.entity.position, { y: 3 }, { duration: 0.5 }).finished; this.entity.color = ...

Resolves after `seconds` of scaled game time (like after()); never resolves if this entity is destroyed first or the scene unloads, so `await this.wait(1); this.entity.x = 0` needs no alive check. Example: await this.wait(0.5).

members.sig: on(name: string, fn: (data: any, source: Entity | null) => void): () => void
members.doc: Subscribe to world events for this behaviour; returns unsubscribe.

Once, the first time the entity is active in the hierarchy (props already applied), before its first update and before the frame is drawn. The instance exists (entity.behaviour) from the moment the entity is spawned or its scene is loaded, active or not; an entity spawned inactive gets onStart when something sets active = true.

Every time the entity becomes active in the hierarchy (it or an ancestor got active = true) while the Script is enabled; the first time it runs right after onStart. Runs before the frame is drawn, so a panel can refresh its texts here and they are right in the first drawn frame.
Every time the entity stops being active (it or an ancestor got active = false, or the Script was disabled), and before onDestroy of an entity that was active. Runs before the frame is drawn.
Every frame; dt in seconds scaled by time.scale.
Every fixed step, before physics.
After all updates.
Before the entity is removed.

items.doc: Entity lookup, spawning and events.

members.doc: Finds by stable id first, then by name. Skips an entity that was destroyed this frame (entity.destroy() takes effect at the end of the frame, but the entity is not found from the call on).
Every entity with this name, in creation order. Skips the ones destroyed this frame.
All alive entities in creation order, without the ones destroyed this frame.

Creates an entity from scene-file JSON ({ name, tags, components }). Vectors in component fields may be Vec2/Vec3, {x,y,z} objects or arrays (2D values get z = 0). The Script behaviour is constructed immediately (entity.behaviour), onStart runs before its first update.

members.sig: spawnPrefab(path: string, opts?: SpawnOptions & { overrides?: Json; childOverrides?: Record<string, Json> }): Entity
members.doc: Instantiates a prefab file. `props` is merged into Script.props; `overrides` is entity JSON merged over the prefab (components deep-merge). `childOverrides` patches the prefab's descendants: key = a child's id, name or path like "Panel/Title", value = { name?, tags?, active?, components? }; an unknown child or field throws with a suggestion.

members.sig: emit(name: string, data?: any, source?: Entity): void
members.doc: Queue a game event; delivered to onEvent and world.on listeners.

members.sig: on(name: string, fn: (data: any, source: Entity | null) => void): () => void
members.doc: Subscribe to an event; returns unsubscribe. The UI sends ui.click, ui.change, ui.submit, ui.focus and ui.cancel with data { id, value? } and the widget as `source` (ui.on wraps them). ui.scale and ui.textScale send ui.scale and ui.textScale with data { value, previous } and no source when the interface scale or the text size changes.
Scene settings (gravity2D, ambientLight, ...).
Simulated seconds since the scene started.

items.name: MouseAPI
items.doc: Mouse state (design-resolution pixels, top-left origin).

members.doc: Position in world coordinates through the main camera.

Wheel notches turned this frame (positive = away from the player). It reads 0 on a frame where the wheel scrolled a ScrollList under the pointer (ui.wheelConsumed is true then): the UI runs before scripts and keeps that wheel for itself.

Whether the mouse cursor is drawn over the window (default true). Set false for a game that draws its own cursor or plays with a pad. Independent of `locked`. A headless run or test only records the value.

Mouse lock for mouse-look cameras: the cursor is hidden and held in the window, `position` stays frozen and `delta` reports raw movement (not design pixels). The window system may unlock it when the window loses focus; the engine locks it again when focus comes back. A headless run or test only records the value.

items.name: GamepadAPI
items.doc: One gamepad, from input.gamepad(index). Raw device state for local multiplayer; actions bound to Gamepad* names already match any pad.

members.doc: A pad is plugged in at this index.

The family of the pad: "xbox", "playstation", "nintendo", "steamdeck" or "generic" (also for a pad that is not connected). Found from its vendor id and name where the platform tells (Windows: XInput pads are xbox; Linux and macOS/iOS: from the ids or names; Android always "generic"). Use input.buttonName() to get the label, not this.

The stable id of the pad in this slot: the same physical pad gives the same id every time it is plugged in (see game.on("gamepadConnected") for what goes into it on each platform). "" for a slot that never had a pad; kept after the pad is unplugged until another pad takes the slot.
What the OS calls the pad ("Wireless Controller", "Xbox controller (XInput)"); "" for a slot that never had a pad; kept after the pad is unplugged.
Button held. Unknown names throw with a suggestion.
Went down this frame.
Went up this frame (also when the pad was unplugged).
Stick -1..1 (+Y up) or trigger 0..1 with the deadzone applied, the same value the action bindings use (sticks: radial deadzone, the rest rescaled to the full range).
The axis as the device reported it, without the deadzone.

items.name: PlayerInputAPI
items.doc: One local player, from input.player(index): the project's input actions (the same names input.down() takes) read through that player's own devices, for games where two to four people share the machine. The devices are a gamepad (pad bindings read only that pad) and/or a key scheme (key bindings read only the keys of that scheme, such as the left half of the keyboard); mouse and touch bindings belong to the shared pointer and players do not read them. A player with no device reads nothing. input.down() and the rest of the global API keep hearing every device. Each player has its own bindings: the defaults are the project's, filtered to the device, and rebind() changes this player only.

members.doc: The player number, 0 to 3.

members.sig: use(device?: { pad?: number; padId?: string; keys?: string } | null): void
members.doc: Gives the player its devices; every field left out means none, and use() or use(null) takes them all away. pad is a gamepad slot (0..3); padId is the stable id of a pad (input.gamepad(i).id) and makes the player follow that pad when it comes back in another slot (it reads nothing while that pad is unplugged); use one of the two. keys names a key scheme: "all" (every key), "left" (the left half: Q W E R T A S D F G Z X C V B, 1-5, Space, Tab, LeftShift...), "right" (the right half: arrows, Enter, Backspace, U I O P H J K L N M, 6-0, punctuation...) or one from factoria.json input.schemes (input.keySchemes() lists them). A bad slot, an unknown scheme (with "did you mean"), or both pad and padId throws and changes nothing. What the player rebound stays with the player when its device changes.

members.sig: readonly device: { pad: number; padId: string; keys: string; slot: number }
members.doc: What use() was given (pad -1, padId "" and keys "" for none) and slot, the pad the player reads right now (-1 for no pad, or for a padId pad that is unplugged).
The pad slot the player reads now (device.slot); -1 for none.
The action is held on this player's devices (analog bindings count from 0.5). Unknown actions throw with a suggestion; a player with no device gives false.
Went down this frame on this player's devices.
Went up this frame on this player's devices.
0..1 strength of the action on this player's devices (the maximum over its bindings).
-1..1 from two actions: value(positive) - value(negative), on this player's devices.

members.sig: vector(left: string, right: string, down: string, up: string): Vec2
members.doc: 2D vector from four actions (+Y up), normalized only when longer than 1, on this player's devices.

The player's bindings of an action, as names rebind() accepts. With a family: only that list ("keys": the keys of its scheme, "pad": gamepad bindings), also when the player has no such device now. Without: the lists of the devices the player has, keys first. The defaults are the project's bindings of the action that belong to the player's scheme (a key scheme may give its own with input.schemes.<name>.actions) and to a pad.

members.sig: rebind(action: string, bindings: string[], family?: "keys" | "pad"): void
members.doc: Replaces this player's bindings of one action, for one family: all the names must be keys ("Space", "W", or a chord of them such as "Ctrl+Z") or all gamepad bindings ("GamepadA", "GamepadLeftStickUp"), or pass the family (an empty array then unbinds that family; without a family it unbinds both). Keys must belong to the player's key scheme (outside it they would not count), and mouse and touch names are refused because the pointer is shared. All or nothing: an unknown action or binding, a key outside the scheme, or a name of the other family throws with "did you mean" and changes nothing. Other players and the global input.rebind() are unaffected.
Puts this player's bindings of one action, or of every action, back to the defaults.

Like input.lastPressed() but only for this player's devices (a chord included, "Ctrl+Z", when the player's scheme has the modifier): a key of its scheme, a button or a stick of its pad that went down this frame, else null. For a "press a key to rebind" screen.

members.sig: export(): { keys?: Record<string, string[]>; pad?: Record<string, string[]> }
members.doc: What the player rebound, for the game to save with storage.set(): only the actions that differ from the defaults ({} when nothing). The device is not part of it.

members.sig: import(data?: { keys?: Record<string, string[]>; pad?: Record<string, string[]> }): string[]
members.doc: Replaces the player's rebinds with what export() gave. An entry that is no longer valid (an action the project dropped, a name that is not a binding or is of the other family) is skipped and described in the returned array (empty when all applied); the rest applies. No data (or {}) resets the player.

items.name: InputAPI
items.doc: Input through named actions (factoria.json input.actions), raw keys or gamepads.

members.doc: Action held. For an analog binding (gamepad stick or trigger) it means value >= 0.5. Unknown actions throw with a suggestion.
Went down this frame.

0..1 strength of an action: 0 or 1 for keys, mouse, touch and pad buttons; for gamepad half-axis and trigger bindings the push after the deadzone (the maximum over the action's bindings). Unknown actions throw with a suggestion.
-1..1 from two actions: value(positive) - value(negative). Analog with a gamepad stick bound to the actions; keys give exactly -1, 0 or 1.

members.sig: vector(left: string, right: string, down: string, up: string): Vec2
members.doc: 2D vector from four actions (+Y up), normalized only when longer than 1: a half-tilted stick gives a short vector, two keys a unit diagonal.
Pad 0..3 (default 0); a bad index throws.
How many players input.player() has: 4 (one per gamepad slot).

Player 0..3 for local multiplayer: the same actions as input.down() but read from that player's own gamepad and/or key scheme (see PlayerInputAPI). Assign devices with input.player(i).use({pad: i}) or use({keys: "left"}); a player with no device reads nothing. A bad index throws. The game assigns devices each time its scene starts (a test starts with none, like it starts with the project's bindings).
The key schemes input.player(i).use({keys}) accepts: "all", "left", "right" and the ones in factoria.json input.schemes.
The keys of a key scheme, as key names. An unknown scheme throws with a suggestion.
Deadzone of gamepad sticks (radial) and triggers, 0 up to 1 (not included); factoria.json input.deadzone sets the start value (default 0.2). Assign to offer calibration in an options menu.

The characters typed this frame, as UTF-8 text ("" when none): from the keyboard or the on-screen keyboard, control characters left out. Append it to a text field's string; handle Backspace and Enter with input.keyPressed(). Desktop and iOS deliver composed text (shift, dead keys, IME). Android delivers what a key types in its layout (letters, digits, punctuation, accents through dead keys): a keyboard app that composes words or emoji (CJK input, emoji) cannot be received by a NativeActivity. docs/MOBILE.md lists the limits.

Shows (default) or hides the on-screen keyboard of phones and tablets while a text field has focus; its characters arrive in input.text. Desktop ignores it, a headless run only records it (input.keyboardShown). A text field does this by itself when it gets and loses focus.
The last value given to showKeyboard() (false at start).

This frame's press of `action` is handled: until the next frame input.pressed() reads false for it and for every other action that shares one of its bindings that went down (Escape is both "pause" and "ui_cancel"). Only the press is taken: down() and value() keep reading the held input, and players (input.player(i)) are not affected. The UI runs before scripts and consumes ui_submit when it clicks a focused Button or Toggle, ui_cancel when a drag took it or when a ui.on("cancel") handler returns true. Call it in your own handler when you take a press that another script would also act on. Unknown actions throw with a suggestion. Example: ui.on("cancel", () => { if (!dialog.open) return false; dialog.close(); return true; });

True while the player is typing text: a TextField has the focus (the engine sets it) or a script turned it on. Actions bound to printable keys (letters, digits, Space, punctuation, alone or with Shift; not Enter, Escape, arrows, F keys or Ctrl/Alt/Super chords) read as not down, pressed or released meanwhile for those bindings, so typing P in a save-name field does not pause. Assigning true is for a script's own text entry (the menu kit's on-screen keyboard); assigning false only clears the script's flag, a focused TextField keeps the mode on. A scene load clears the script's flag.

True while the platform shows its own keyboard for the focused text field, because a native plugin took it (the Steam Deck's keyboard, through the Steam plugin); false otherwise. Only a gamepad player's focus can start it. The menu kit's on-screen keyboard stays closed while it is true. Read-only.

The system Back button or gesture of Android (nothing else sends it; a test sends it with game.pressBack()). Handlers run newest first at the start of the frame; the first one that does not return false consumes the press, so a handler that closes a menu returns true (or nothing) and one that has nothing to close returns false. When no handler consumes it, or there is none, the game quits, which is what Back did before this event existed. A handler that throws is reported and counts as consumed. Handlers end with the scene, like ui.on. Returns the function that removes the handler. Example: input.onBack(() => { if (!menu.open) return false; menu.close(); return true; });

One pulse of the vibration motor of a phone, seconds above 0 and up to 5 (default 0.1): 0.02 to 0.05 is a tap, 0.2 a buzz. iOS cannot pick a length: a short pulse is a haptic tap, a long one the system vibration; iPads have no motor. Android needs the VIBRATE permission, which the FactorIA Android template declares. A no-op on desktop; a headless run or test records the pulse (game.vibrations()). Throws for anything but a number in range.
The names of all input actions (from factoria.json input.actions and the engine's own), sorted.
The bindings of an action in order, as names input.rebind() accepts: ["Space", "W", "GamepadA"]. An unknown action throws with a suggestion.

Replaces the bindings of an existing action, for a controls screen. Names are keys ("Space", "W", "Left"), "MouseLeft", "MouseRight", "MouseMiddle", "Touch" and gamepad bindings ("GamepadA", "GamepadLeftStickUp", "GamepadRightTrigger"...), case-insensitive. A key, mouse button or Touch takes modifiers joined by "+": "Ctrl+Z", "Shift+MouseLeft", "Ctrl+Shift+S" (Ctrl, Shift, Alt, Super; each means either side's key); a chord is stored and printed back as Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Super+input, and a malformed one ("Cntrl+Z", "Ctrl+", "Ctrl+GamepadA") throws saying which part is wrong and what to write instead. When another action binds the plain input, the chord wins: Z does not fire while Ctrl is held if some action binds Ctrl+Z. All or nothing: an unknown action or binding name throws an Error with "did you mean" and nothing changes. An empty array unbinds the action. Several actions may share a binding. Combine with input.lastPressed() to let the player press the new key, and save input.bindings(action) with storage.set() to restore it at the next start (see docs/SCRIPTING.md).
Puts one action (or every action when no name is given) back to what factoria.json and the engine's defaults say, undoing input.rebind().

The binding that went down this frame ("Space", "MouseLeft", "Touch", "GamepadA", "GamepadLeftStickUp"...) or null: for a "press a key to rebind" screen. With modifiers held it is the chord ("Ctrl+Z", "Shift+MouseLeft"), ready for rebind(). A modifier pressed alone ("LeftShift") is reported when it is released, so pressing Ctrl on the way to Ctrl+Z does not end the wait; a modifier that something else was pressed with is not reported by itself. Sticks and triggers count when pushed past half way. If several went down in the same frame, keys come first, then touch, mouse buttons, pad buttons, sticks and triggers. Ignore the frame in which the player clicked the Rebind button itself.

The device that produced input last: "keyboard" (a key going down), "mouse" (moved, clicked, wheel), "gamepad" (a button pressed or a stick pushed past the deadzone) or "touch". "keyboard" at the start. Show gamepad prompts when it is "gamepad".

The label a player sees, for button prompts: a key gives its name ("Space", "W"), the mouse "Left Click", and a pad button the name on THAT pad (pad 0 by default): Xbox/Steam Deck "A" "B" "X" "Y" "LB" "RB" "LT" "RT" "View" "Menu", PlayStation "Cross" "Circle" "Square" "Triangle" "L1" "R1" "L2" "R2" "Create" "Options", Nintendo "B" "A" "Y" "X" "L" "R" "ZL" "ZR" "-" "+" (our A, the bottom button, is Nintendo's B). An action gives the label of its first binding for input.lastDevice (a pad binding after pad input, else a key or mouse binding), or "" if it has no binding. Unknown names throw with a suggestion.

Raw key by name ("Space", "A", "Escape"...), or a modifier by name: "Ctrl", "Shift", "Alt" and "Super" are held while either side's key is ("LeftShift" is the left key only). A chord in an action binding ("Ctrl+Z") is read with input.down(action), not here.
True on the frame the key went down; takes the same names as keyDown, "Ctrl" and the other modifiers included (either side).
True on the frame the key went up; takes the same names as keyDown, "Ctrl" and the other modifiers included (either side).

Project-relative clip path.
The bus it plays on.

A subtitle for this sound, plain text. It shows on the Captions component while the sound plays and goes when the sound ends or is stopped (audio.stop, audio.stopAll). With no Captions entity it is only tracked (game.captions() in tests). Use captionKey for a text that follows the language.

items.name: AudioBus
items.doc: A handle on one audio bus, from audio.bus(name): its effects (docs/SCRIPTING.md, "Audio buses"). Every method returns the handle, so audio.bus("music").lowpass(800).reverb(0.2) chains. A bus with no effect does no effect work (it only costs one add per sample into the master while it plays).

members.doc: The bus this handle controls.

members.sig: lowpass(hz: number | null, opts?: { fade?: number }): AudioBus
members.doc: A 12 dB per octave low-pass filter at `hz` (20..20000; a muffled, underwater sound is 400..800). 0 or null switches it off. With `fade` (seconds) the cutoff slides (in octaves) from where it is; a bus with no filter starts open. Costs one biquad per channel: five multiply-adds per sample of the bus.

members.sig: reverb(mix: number, opts?: { fade?: number }): AudioBus
members.doc: A small room reverb: the bus is heard as (1 - mix) dry + mix wet, mix 0..1 (0 switches it off, 0.3 is a touch of room). The tail rings out for about 4 seconds after the bus goes silent, then the work stops. With `fade` the mix slides. Costs several times a low-pass (eight comb and four all-pass filters per channel) and some memory for its delay lines.

members.sig: duck(byBus: string | null, amount?: number, attack?: number, release?: number): AudioBus
members.doc: Lowers this bus by `amount` (the fraction removed, 0.5 default: half as loud) while `byBus` is louder than -40 dBFS, e.g. audio.bus("music").duck("sfx", 0.5) pushes the music down under every sound effect. `attack` (0.05 s) and `release` (0.5 s) are time constants in seconds: the bus covers 63% of the way down (or back up) in that time, about 95% in three times it. null switches ducking off (so does unduck()); the master cannot duck. Costs a peak detector on `byBus` and one multiply per sample here.
Switches ducking off.

members.sig: volume(volume: number, opts?: { fade?: number }): AudioBus
members.doc: The bus volume, like audio.setVolume (the player's volume: snapshots scale on top of it and leave it alone). With `fade` (seconds) it moves in a straight line; without it, it still ramps over about 10 ms so it does not click.

members.sig: state(): { volume: number, snapshotVolume: number, lowpass: number, reverb: number, duck: { by: string, amount: number, attack: number, release: number } | null }
members.doc: The settings the bus is moving to (a fade in progress shows its end value): `lowpass` is 0 when off, `snapshotVolume` is the scale the last snapshot put on `volume`.

items.name: AudioAPI
items.doc: Sound playback.

members.doc: Plays a clip, returns a voice id. With caption / captionKey the sound also shows a subtitle on the Captions component for as long as it plays (docs/TEXT.md, "Captions").

The sounds that play now, oldest first: { id, path, bus, volume, pitch, pan, loop, music, source }. `volume` is the voice volume it is moving to; `music` is true for the music and its layers; `source` is the entity id of an AudioSource, "" for scripts. Use it to count or limit voices on a bus, e.g. audio.activeVoices().filter((v) => v.bus === "ambience").length.
Stops every sound and the music now, a persisted track included.

members.sig: music(path: string, opts?: { volume?: number; fade?: number; persist?: boolean }): void
members.doc: Starts looping background music on the "music" bus (volume default 0.6, fade-in `fade` seconds default 0.5). The same track already playing is only retuned. A scene load (scene.load, reload) stops every sound and the music, and then starts the new scene's SceneSettings.music, even when it is the same track as before; with persist: true this track keeps playing through scene loads (a scene whose SceneSettings.music is the same track does not restart it; another track replaces it). Example: audio.music("assets/theme.ogg", { persist: true }).

members.sig: musicLayers(layers: Record<string, string>, opts?: { volume?: number; fade?: number; persist?: boolean; levels?: Record<string, number> }): boolean
members.doc: Starts layered music: `layers` maps a layer name to a clip path. Every layer starts on the same audio sample and loops, so layers of equal length stay aligned; clips of different lengths drift by their length difference at each loop. `levels` gives each layer's starting level 0..1 (default 1), `volume` scales all (default 0.6). Replaces the current music. Returns false, and plays nothing, when a clip cannot be loaded. stopMusic stops every layer; a scene load stops them unless persist: true. The play log has one entry per layer, with `layer` set. Example: audio.musicLayers({ base: "assets/m/base.ogg", drums: "assets/m/drums.ogg" }, { levels: { drums: 0 } }); later audio.setLayer("drums", 1, 2).

members.sig: setLayer(name: string, level: number, fade?: number): void
members.doc: Moves a layer of the music started by musicLayers to `level` (0 = silent, 1 = full) in a straight line over `fade` seconds (default 0: at once). Throws, listing the layers, when there is no such layer.

members.sig: setVoiceVolume(voice: number, volume: number, fade?: number): boolean
members.doc: Changes the volume of a sound that plays (an id from audio.play), over `fade` seconds (default 0: at once); bus and master volumes still apply on top. Returns false when the voice is not playing (it ended or was stopped). Example: const id = audio.play("assets/wind.ogg", { loop: true, volume: 0 }); audio.setVoiceVolume(id, 1, 3).
Stops the music (and every layer) fading out over `fade` seconds (default 0.5).

Volume multiplier of a bus (0 = silent, 1 = as recorded; default 1 for every bus). A bus from factoria.json "audio"."buses" works too (SCRIPTING.md, "Project buses"). Plays go to "sfx" unless their `bus` option says otherwise; "master" scales everything. The setting is not saved: an options menu stores it (storage) and sets it again at start.
The volume last set for a bus with setVolume (1 when never set). Throws for an unknown bus name.

A handle on a bus to set its effects: low-pass, reverb, ducking and volume (see AudioBus). Throws for an unknown name, with a "did you mean". The effects stay across scene loads, like volumes (a snapshot or the handle changes them).

members.sig: snapshot(name: string, opts?: { fade?: number }): void
members.doc: Moves every bus to the named snapshot of factoria.json "audio"."snapshots" (volume scale, low-pass, reverb and ducking; a bus the snapshot does not list goes back to neutral, so { "normal": {} } is the way back). `fade` is the seconds the move takes; without it the snapshot's own "fade" (0.5 when it has none). Low-pass, reverb and volume slide, ducking switches at once; the volumes the player set with setVolume are not touched. Throws for an unknown name, with a "did you mean". `factoria validate` checks the catalog.
The snapshot names of factoria.json and the one applied last ("" = none).

members.doc: Agent radius of this query (meters). Default: the NavMesh3D's agentRadius. Larger than that is an error: bake a NavMesh3D for the bigger agent.
How far (meters) a start or goal that is not on walkable ground is moved onto the nearest walkable cell (default agentRadius + 2 cells).
When the goal cannot be reached, return a path to the reachable point nearest to it (complete = false) instead of found = false.
Id of the entity with the NavMesh3D to use. Default: the first enabled one that contains `from`.

Id of the NavMesh3D entity that answered.

Number of rows.

members.sig: setCost(col: number, row: number, cost: number | null): void
members.doc: Changes the cost of entering one cell (>= 0; Infinity, a negative number or null blocks it). Throws for a cell outside the grid. Flow fields built on this grid are rebuilt the next time they are asked. Example: grid.setCost(3, 4, Infinity); // a wall went up
The cost of entering the cell, Infinity when it is blocked. Throws for a cell outside the grid.
Replaces every cost at once (width * height numbers, row-major, row 0 = top).

members.doc: Allow 8-way steps (default false), with the same rules as nav.findTilePath: a diagonal costs sqrt(2) times the cell entered and never cuts a corner.

items.name: NavFlowField
items.doc: The cost to the nearest of some goal cells, for every cell of a NavGrid (nav.flowField). One search serves every walker heading for those goals. It reads the grid it was made on: after grid.setCost, the next question rebuilds it.

members.doc: The grid the field reads.
The goal cells.
Whether steps may be diagonal.
How many times the field has been searched so far (1 after the first question, +1 for every question that follows a change of the grid).
The cost of the cheapest route from the cell to the nearest goal (the entering costs of the cells after it; 0 at a goal), Infinity when no goal can be reached or the cell is outside the grid.

members.sig: stepToward(col: number, row: number): NavCell | null
members.doc: The next cell on the cheapest route to the nearest goal, in O(1) (ties go east, south, west, north, then the diagonals), or null at a goal, where no goal can be reached and outside the grid. Example: const n = field.stepToward(this.col, this.row); if (n) { this.col = n.col; this.row = n.row; }
All the cells from this one to the goal it reaches, both ends included (what repeated stepToward gives); empty when no goal can be reached.

items.name: NavAPI
items.doc: Path finding: on the baked NavMesh3D (docs/NAVIGATION.md) and over tile maps (findTilePath).

members.sig: findPath(from: Vec3 | { x: number; y: number; z: number } | readonly [number, number, number], to: Vec3Like, opts?: NavPathOptions): NavPath
members.doc: Shortest walkable path between two 3D points (the agent's feet), as a few corner points on the ground: around walls, up ramps, never up a step higher than NavMesh3D.stepHeight. Never throws for 'no route': check `found` (off-mesh and disconnected results explain themselves in message / hint). Throws an Error that explains the fix when the scene has no NavMesh3D or opts.radius is bigger than the mesh was baked for. Deterministic. Example: const p = nav.findPath(this.entity.position, player.position, { radius: 0.3 }); if (p.found) this.target = p.points[1] ?? p.points[0];

Builds a cost grid that stays native: nav.findTilePath(grid, from, to) and nav.flowField(grid, goals) reuse it, and grid.setCost(col, row, cost) changes one cell. Use it when you ask for many routes on one map (hundreds of walkers on a road grid). Throws when width / height are not whole numbers >= 1 or cost does not hold width * height entries. Example: const grid = nav.createGrid({ width: 60, height: 60, cost: roads.map((r) => (r ? 1 : Infinity)) }); grid.setCost(3, 4, 1); // a road was built

members.sig: flowField(grid: NavGrid, goals: NavCell | readonly [number, number] | readonly (NavCell | readonly [number, number])[], opts?: NavFlowFieldOptions): NavFlowField
members.doc: The cost to the nearest of one or more goal cells from every cell of the grid, computed once (when first asked, again after the grid changed): field.stepToward(col, row) then gives the next cell in O(1), field.distance(col, row) the cost, field.pathFrom(col, row) the whole way. Many walkers heading for the same goal share one field, which is much cheaper than one findTilePath per walker. Same cost rules as findTilePath; a blocked goal cell is entered at cost 1. Throws for a grid that is not from nav.createGrid, no goals, or a goal outside the grid. Example: const field = nav.flowField(grid, [{ col: 9, row: 4 }]); const n = field.stepToward(this.col, this.row);

members.sig: findTilePath(map: Entity | string | NavGrid | NavTileGrid | NavGrid, from: NavCell | readonly [number, number], to: NavCell | readonly [number, number], opts?: NavTileOptions): NavTilePath
members.doc: A* over the cells of a Tilemap (the entity or its id: solidTiles block, other cells cost 1, opts.costs changes that per tile) or of your own grid { width, height, cost } or a grid kept natively by nav.createGrid (the fast form for many queries on one map: the array form converts and sweeps the whole map on every call). 4-way by default; opts.diagonals allows 8-way without cutting corners. Deterministic (same query, same path) and no JS callback per cell: put the rules in the costs. Never throws for 'no route': check `found` (reason, message and hint explain). Throws when the map or a cell is not what the call expects. Example: const p = nav.findTilePath(world.find("ground"), { col: 1, row: 1 }, { col: 8, row: 5 }, { costs: { 4: 5 }, diagonals: true }); if (p.found) this.target = p.points[1] ?? p.points[0];

A counter of the changes to the Tilemap's tiles. Compare it with the value from when you searched to know a cached path is stale. It goes up on setTile / tilemap.set_tile and on any write that replaces `tiles` (a script assigning tilemap.tiles, scene.set_component, the editor); it starts at 0 on every scene load and each call costs one pass over the tiles.

members.sig: bake(mesh?: string): { mesh: string; cellsX: number; cellsZ: number; cells: number; spans: number; walkableCells: number; regions: number; obstacles: number }[]
members.doc: Bakes the NavMesh3D of entity `mesh` (default every enabled one) now and returns its stats. Needed only when autoBake is off; the colliders are re-baked by themselves otherwise.

Example: physics.shapeCast({ shape: "box", size: [16, 24] }, vec2(x, y), vec2(x, y - 40), { ignore: this.entity }). items.name: CameraAPI
items.doc: Camera helpers. A game draws every active camera with primary = true, in ascending depth, each into its own rectangle of the screen (Camera.viewport): a split screen is two or more such cameras. The conversions take the camera to use; without one they use the camera whose viewport contains the point, or the first camera for a world point.

members.doc: The first camera drawn (the lowest depth among the active cameras with primary = true), or null when there is none. In a split screen it is player one's camera; use `all` or `at` for the others.
Every camera drawn, in draw order (ascending depth, equal depths in the order they were created); at most 8 are drawn. One entry for a game with a single camera.

The camera whose viewport contains the screen point `v` (design pixels): where two viewports overlap, the one drawn last. A point outside every viewport gives the first camera; null when no camera is active. Use it to pick which player a click belongs to.

members.sig: worldToScreen(v: Vec3Like, camera?: Entity | string): Vec2
members.doc: Where the world point `v` appears on the screen (design pixels, top-left origin) as seen by `camera` (default: the first camera drawn). The result is inside that camera's viewport when the point is in its view.

members.sig: screenToWorld(v: Vec2Like, depth?: number | Entity | string, camera?: Entity | string): Vec3
members.doc: The world point under the screen point `v` (design pixels). `depth` is the world z of a 2D view (default 0), or the distance along the ray of a perspective view. `camera` defaults to the camera whose viewport contains `v`, else the first camera; the camera may also be given as the second argument: screenToWorld(v, cam).

members.sig: screenRay(v: Vec2Like, camera?: Entity | string): { origin: Vec3; direction: Vec3 }
members.doc: The ray under the screen point `v` (design pixels) through `camera` (default: the camera whose viewport contains `v`, else the first camera). For a 3D pick: physics.raycast(origin, origin + direction * distance).

Pixels per world unit of an orthographic camera (design pixels one world unit covers), the zoom of a strategy camera: the viewport height in design pixels / 2 / orthoSize; 1 when orthoSize is 0 (pixel perfect on a full-screen viewport). `camera` defaults to the first camera drawn. Throws without a camera or for a perspective one.

members.sig: setZoom(zoom: number, camera?: Entity | string): void
members.doc: Sets the camera's zoom in pixels per world unit by writing Camera.orthoSize = (viewport height in design pixels) / 2 / zoom, so a game never derives orthoSize from its design height by hand. Throws for a zoom that is not a positive number. Example: camera.setZoom(1.5); // 1.5 pixels per world unit

The Camera.orthoSize that shows the world at `zoom` pixels per world unit on a screen `designHeight` design pixels high: designHeight / 2 / zoom. Defaults: zoom 1 and the design height of the screen (screen.size.y). Pure, it changes nothing.

members.sig: zoomAt(screenPoint: Vec2Like, factor: number, options?: { camera?: Entity | string; min?: number; max?: number }): number
members.doc: Zooms in by `factor` (2 doubles the pixels per world unit, 0.5 halves them) and moves the camera so the world point under `screenPoint` (design pixels) stays under it: zoom towards the cursor. `min` and `max` clamp the resulting zoom (pixels per world unit, see zoomOf); the camera is the one under the point unless `options.camera` names one. Returns the zoom now. It does not keep the view inside the map: call clampTo after. A 2D helper: the camera must be orthographic and not rotated. Throws for a factor that is not a positive number. Example: camera.zoomAt(input.mouse.position, 1.15 ** input.mouse.wheel, { min: 0.4, max: 2.5 });

members.sig: panBy(screenDelta: Vec2Like, camera?: Entity | string): void
members.doc: Moves the camera so the world follows a screen movement, as a drag does: a delta of (10, 0) leaves the world 10 design pixels further right on the screen (the camera moves left in the world); +Y of the delta is down the screen. Takes the delta in design pixels whatever the zoom, e.g. camera.panBy(input.mouse.delta) while a button is held.

members.sig: clampTo(rect: RectLike, options?: { camera?: Entity | string; margin?: number }): void
members.doc: Moves the camera as little as needed so the view stays inside the world rectangle `rect` ({ x, y, w, h } with (x, y) the bottom-left corner, like entity.bounds()), grown by `margin` world units. On an axis where the view is wider than the rectangle the camera is centred on it. Example: camera.clampTo(world.find("map").bounds(), { margin: 100 });

items.name: DebugAPI
items.doc: Immediate-mode debug drawing (one frame).

members.sig: line(a: Vec3Like, b: Vec3Like, color?: ColorLike): void
rect(x: number, y: number, w: number, h: number, color?: ColorLike): void

members.doc: Rect as { x, y, w, h } or [x, y, w, h].

members.sig: circle(center: Vec2Like, radius: number, color?: ColorLike): void
text(screenPos: Vec2Like, text: string, color?: ColorLike): void
box(center: Vec3Like, size: Vec3Like, color?: ColorLike): void
sphere(center: Vec3Like, radius: number, color?: ColorLike): void

members.doc: Draws the Bone2D entities of `root` and everything under it for one frame (every bone of the scene when `root` is left out): a thin kite from each bone's origin to its tip and a dot at the origin, in world space, so the skeleton shows while the clip or IK2D poses it. Call it every frame from onUpdate. Example: debug.bones(world.find("hip"), [1, 0.5, 0, 1]);

Reads a scene's files into memory ahead of time, a little every frame, and returns a handle at once: scene.load(path) of a preloaded scene reads nothing from the disk, so a loading screen can draw (and animate) while the next level loads. Reads the scene file and what it points at: prefabs, materials, textures, models (a .gltf brings its .bin and images), audio and fonts. Per frame the work is cut in whole files: four files per frame in tests, headless runs and replays (so the frames it takes never depend on how fast the machine is), as many as fit in a few milliseconds (at least one) in a game with a window. A scene path that does not exist throws with a did-you-mean list. Example: const job = scene.preload("scenes/level2.scene.json"); in onUpdate: bar.width = 400 * job.progress; if (job.done) scene.load("scenes/level2.scene.json"); or job.promise.then(() => scene.load(...)).

Deferred to the end of the frame. `props` (a plain JSON object) is what the new scene reads with game.sceneProps(), from its first onStart. A load without props gives the new scene {}; scene.reload() keeps the current props. Example: scene.load("scenes/level.scene.json", { level: 3 }).
The path of the running scene. A reload of the same scene leaves it equal: use `generation` to tell the two apart.

Counts the scene loads: it changes on every load (scene.load, scene.reload, game.load in a test), a reload of the same scene included, and never goes back. A script that awaits something (a timeline, a preload, a platform answer) keeps `const gen = scene.generation` and drops the answer when `scene.generation !== gen`; that also catches a reload, which `scene.current` and a held entity handle of the old load cannot tell from the scene itself. Example: `const gen = scene.generation; await cutscene.play(); if (scene.generation !== gen) return;`.

items.name: ScreenInsets
items.doc: How far a notch, rounded corners and the system bars cover the screen from each edge, in design pixels.

items.name: ScreenAPI
items.doc: The screen as the player sees it, in design pixels with the origin at the top-left and +Y down (like screen-space Text and UI). On a phone the safe area is the screen minus the notch, rounded corners and the system bars; everywhere else (desktop, headless, tests without game.setSafeArea) it is the whole screen. It follows rotation. Give HUD items `safeArea: true` to anchor them to it without any script.

members.doc: The design resolution (the same as game.screenSize).
{ left, top, right, bottom }: the distance in design pixels the notch, corners and bars cover from each edge. All 0 on a screen without cutouts.

The part of the screen to keep text and buttons in, as a Rect { x, y, w, h } in design pixels: (x, y) is its TOP-LEFT corner and y grows downwards (unlike entity.bounds(), which is in the +Y-up world). Read it every frame or when needed: it changes when the phone rotates. Example: const a = screen.safeArea; button.position = [a.x + a.w - 20, a.y + 20];

True while time.scale is 0. Setting it true sets time.scale to 0 (physics, particles, animators, timers and onUpdate stop; runWhilePaused behaviours and the UI keep running), false restores the time.scale it had when it was set true (1 if it was already 0). Setting time.scale while paused changes the scale to restore, the game stays paused.

The props the current scene was started with: scene.load(path, props), factoria run --props, or the scene.load command's props. A plain object, {} when none were given; available from the first onStart. A reload keeps them, a load without props drops them. A fresh copy each call. Example: const level = game.sceneProps().level ?? 1.

members.sig: today(): { readonly year: number; readonly month: number; readonly day: number; readonly weekday: number; readonly hour: number; readonly minute: number; readonly second: number; readonly utcOffsetMinutes: number; readonly iso: string; readonly utc: { readonly year: number; readonly month: number; readonly day: number; readonly iso: string } }
members.doc: The calendar date: year, month (1-12), day, weekday (0 = Sunday .. 6 = Saturday), hour, minute and second (the local time of day), utcOffsetMinutes (minutes east of UTC), iso ("YYYY-MM-DD") and utc ({ year, month, day, iso }: the date of the same moment in UTC; pass utc.iso as the leaderboards' options.day for one daily board worldwide). THE way to read the date: never use `Date`, whose wall clock makes a run differ from the next (like Math.random, see rng). A game with a window gets the player's real local date and time, read again about once a minute and when the app comes back (game.on("dayChanged") says when the day changes); `factoria test`, headless runs, `factoria call` and the MCP server get a fixed date, 2026-01-01 at 00:00:00 unless --date says another; a replay (--input) plays with the date and time it was recorded on. Tests set it with game.setDate("2026-10-23T23:59:30"). Example: const t = game.today(); rng.seed(t.year * 10000 + t.month * 100 + t.day); for a different challenge every day.

True while the game's window has the keyboard focus (always true on a phone with the app in the foreground, in headless runs and in tests until game.blur()). Changes are announced by game.on("focus") and game.on("blur").

members.sig: on(event: "suspend" | "resume" | "focus" | "blur" | "dayChanged", fn: (today: { readonly iso: string }) => void): () => void
members.doc: Listens to the life of the app: "suspend" (the app goes to the background: the home button on a phone, a call), "resume" (it is back), "focus" and "blur" (the window gains or loses the focus; a desktop window that is covered does not suspend). "dayChanged" (the local calendar day changed while the game ran: past midnight, or the clock was set; a game with a window reads the clock about once a minute) calls fn with game.today(); the other handlers take no arguments. Returns a function that stops listening. Listeners end with the scene, like world.on, so register them where the scene starts (a Behaviour's onStart). With factoria.json "pauseOnSuspend" (default true) the engine also freezes the game and the music while suspended: after the "suspend" handlers ran (a handler that opened your pause menu, game.paused = true, keeps its pause) and before the "resume" ones. Set "pauseOnSuspend": false to decide yourself. Example: game.on("suspend", () => pauseMenu.open());

members.sig: on(event: "gamepadConnected" | "gamepadDisconnected", fn: (pad: { readonly slot: number; readonly id: string; readonly name: string; readonly type: GamepadType }) => void): () => void
members.doc: Listens for a pad being plugged in or out (or paired or lost over Bluetooth). fn gets { slot, id, name, type }: slot is the number input.gamepad(slot) answers for (0 to 3), id is the same for the same physical pad every time (the vendor and product ids, the name and, where the platform has one, a serial number, GUID or device path: use it to give a player their pad back), name is what the OS calls it and type is "xbox", "playstation", "nintendo", "steamdeck" or "generic". A pad that comes back takes the slot it had when that is free (Windows, macOS, iOS, Android and the web; on Linux the kernel's joystick number is the slot). What each platform can put in the id: Windows XInput has no ids, so an XInput pad is "an Xbox pad in XInput slot N" (its id ends with "#xinputN"); Linux adds the kernel's serial (uniq) when the pad has one; macOS and iOS (GameController) and the web (Gamepad.id, no serial: browsers hide it) give the name and, on the web, the vendor and product; Android adds the InputDevice descriptor. Two pads of one model without a serial share an id. Losing the window focus does not disconnect a pad that is still plugged in. Pads already plugged in when the first scene starts are not announced: read input.gamepad(i).connected and .id at the start. Listeners end with the scene, like world.on. Example: game.on("gamepadConnected", (pad) => hud.toast(`${pad.name} is player ${pad.slot + 1}`));

members.sig: on(event: "quit", fn: (event: { readonly cancelled: boolean; cancel(): void }) => void): () => void
members.doc: Listens for the player closing the window (the close button, Cmd+Q, Alt+F4). Desktop windows only: the web and phones never raise it. The handler gets an event whose cancel() keeps the window open (to ask "Really quit?", to save or to send a last analytics event with a short timeout); game.quit() closes it afterwards and does not come back to this handler, so a handler that cancelled can still end the game later. Not raised by game.quit() itself, nor in headless runs (tests simulate it with game.closeWindow()). Returns a function that stops listening; listeners end with the scene. Example: game.on("quit", (e) => { e.cancel(); flush().then(() => game.quit()); });
factoria.json contents.

members.sig: notices(): { name: string; url: string; license: string; usedFor: string }[]
members.doc: The third-party software inside the FactorIA runtime that every game ships (the parts whose full license texts `factoria export` writes to FACTORIA_NOTICES.txt next to the game), FactorIA first. Show it on a credits or licenses screen: e.g. game.notices().map((n) => `${n.name} (${n.license})`).
The platform this runtime was built for. Menus use it for platform rules, e.g. phone and tablet apps have no Quit button (the system closes them).

members.sig: readonly device: Readonly<{ formFactor: "desktop" | "phone" | "tablet"; gpuBackend: string; memoryGB: number; tier: "low" | "medium" | "high"; steamDeck: boolean; handheld: boolean }>
members.doc: The device the game runs on, to pick a graphics preset: formFactor (a phone and a tablet are told apart by the short side of the screen, 600 logical pixels), gpuBackend ("metal", "d3d11", "glcore", "gles3", "wgpu", "vulkan"; "headless" in headless runs and tests), memoryGB (physical memory, 0 when the platform cannot tell) and tier ("low", "medium" or "high", from the graphics backend and the memory: under 3.5 GB low, under 7.5 GB (5.5 on a phone or tablet) medium), steamDeck (true on a Steam Deck: the Steam plugin says so when Steam is running, which is certain; without it the SteamDeck=1 environment variable that Steam sets for games it starts on a Deck decides, and a SteamDeck=0 launch option turns it off; a Deck reports formFactor "desktop") and handheld (true on a Steam Deck, a phone or a tablet: a screen held in the hands, so a game picks bigger text and touch or pad prompts). Headless runs, tests and the editor always read { formFactor: "desktop", gpuBackend: "headless", memoryGB: 8, tier: "high", steamDeck: false, handheld: false } so output never depends on the machine; tests change it with game.setDevice(). Example: const preset = { low: "performance", medium: "balanced", high: "quality" }[game.device.tier].

members.sig: readonly accessibility: Readonly<{ textScale: number; reduceMotion: boolean; highContrast: boolean; screenReader: boolean }>
members.doc: The player's operating system accessibility settings, to start your options screen from: textScale (the system text size, 1 = 100 %, between 0.5 and 4), reduceMotion (animations turned off or reduced), highContrast and screenReader (a screen reader or touch exploration is running). Read when the game starts and again when the window regains focus or the app resumes. The engine applies none of them: apply them to your own options on the first run and save the player's choice (docs/MENUS.md). Where a platform cannot tell, the value is 1 / false: macOS and the web have no text size, the web and Linux outside GNOME have no screen reader. Headless runs, tests and the editor always give { textScale: 1, reduceMotion: false, highContrast: false, screenReader: false }; tests change it with game.setAccessibility(). Example: const size = storage.get("textScale", game.accessibility.textScale).

items.name: WindowMode
items.doc: How the window is shown: windowed (a frame and a size of its own), borderless (no frame, covers the monitor) or fullscreen (covers the monitor; on macOS its own Space). See window.setMode() for what each one means on each OS.

items.name: MonitorInfo
items.doc: One monitor, from window.monitors().

members.doc: Its place in window.monitors(), the number window.setMonitor() takes. The primary monitor is 0.

What the OS calls it ("DELL U2723QE", "Built-in Retina Display", "HDMI-1"; Windows gives the graphics driver's text, often "Generic PnP Monitor"). Two identical monitors have the same name: show the index too.
Its size in logical pixels.
The OS's main monitor (the one with the taskbar or menu bar).
The game window is on it now.

items.name: Resolution
items.doc: A window size in logical pixels, from window.resolutions().

items.name: WindowAPI
items.doc: The game window, for an options menu: full screen, size, vsync and frame cap. The getters work in every run (a run without a window answers from factoria.json display settings). Every setter throws an Error that explains why when this run has no window (headless runs, tests, the MCP server, the editor's game view), so check `window.available` first. The engine saves nothing: keep the player's choice with storage.set() and apply it at start (docs/SCRIPTING.md has the recipe). Sizes are logical pixels: the window system's points, so a 1280 x 720 window on a 200% display has a 2560 x 1440 framebuffer. Phones and tablets always run full screen.

members.doc: True when the game owns a real window: `factoria run`, an exported game, the mobile players. False in headless runs, tests and inside the editor.
Whether the window is full screen (the project's display.fullscreen when there is no window; always true on phones and tablets).

Enters or leaves full screen: `setMode("fullscreen")` for true, `setMode("windowed")` for false. `window.fullscreen` follows at once. On phones and tablets true does nothing and false throws ("phones and tablets always run full screen"). Throws without a window.

"windowed", "borderless" or "fullscreen" ("fullscreen" when the project's display.fullscreen is on and there is no window, and always on phones and tablets). `window.fullscreen` is true for both borderless and fullscreen.

Chooses how the window is shown. "windowed" has a frame and the size window.setSize() gave. "borderless" has no frame and covers the monitor the window is on. "fullscreen" covers it too, and where the OS has a native full screen it uses it: on macOS that is the OS's own full screen Space (the menu bar slides in, Mission Control shows it as a Space; borderless instead hides the menu bar and the Dock but stays on the desktop's Space); on Windows and Linux the engine has no exclusive mode, so fullscreen and borderless are the same frameless window over the monitor and the two names only keep what the player picked. On macOS going from fullscreen straight to borderless throws (the Space takes a moment to leave): go through "windowed" and wait a second. Use window.supports("borderless") before offering borderless. Throws without a window, on an unknown name, and on phones and tablets for anything but "fullscreen".

The monitors, primary first. A run without a window, phones, tablets and the web answer with one entry, the display the game runs on (a run without a window: the project's display size). Linux lists the connected XRandR outputs (one entry for the whole screen when libXrandr is missing).
The index in window.monitors() of the monitor the window is on (0 when there is only one).

Moves the window to monitor `index` of window.monitors(): a windowed window is centred on it, a fullscreen or borderless one covers it. Works on Windows, macOS and Linux; throws on other platforms, without a window, for an index that does not exist, and on macOS while the window is in its native full screen Space (leave it with setMode("windowed") first). `window.displaySize` and `window.resolutions()` describe the new monitor afterwards (on Linux a moment later, when the window manager has moved the window). Check window.supports("monitors") first.
The window's client size in logical pixels (the project's display size when there is no window). In full screen it is the monitor's size.
The size in logical pixels of the monitor the window is on (the whole screen on Linux with several monitors); the window size when the platform cannot tell.

Resizes the window's client area, in whole logical pixels from 160 to 16384; the window keeps its position. Desktop windows only, and not in full screen: call setFullscreen(false) first, or the call throws and says so. The game keeps its design resolution and letterboxes (or expands, see display.scaleMode) to the new size.

Window sizes for a resolution picker: common 16:9 and 16:10 sizes (640x360 up to 3840x2160) plus the game's design size, keeping those that fit the monitor, smallest first. Pass an entry to setSize().
Whether presents wait for the display (the project's display.vsync at start, then setVsync()).

Turns vsync on or off while the game runs (Windows, Linux; macOS only stops waiting for the display). Throws and names the platform where it cannot (phones and tablets, a Linux driver without swap control) or when there is no window.

Frames per second the window may draw at: 0 = unlimited (default), else a whole number from 15 to 1000. The game loop waits so frames do not start faster than that; the simulation still runs at the fixed step, so gameplay results do not change. Useful with vsync off, or to save battery on a laptop. Setting it throws without a window and on phones and tablets (the display sets the pace).

Resolution of the picture as a fraction of the window, from 0.5 to 1 (default 1). 0.5 draws a quarter of the pixels and scales the picture up: the cheapest graphics option on a weak phone. Works in every run with a renderer, headless tests included (game.screenshot then has that size); a run without graphics only remembers the value. A number outside 0.5 - 1 throws. The engine saves nothing: keep the player's choice with storage.set(). Example: window.renderScale = game.device.tier === "low" ? 0.6 : 1.

Whether this run can do `feature`, so an options menu hides what a phone, tablet or test cannot instead of catching the Error: frameCap, fullscreen and resize need a desktop window (window.available and game.device.formFactor "desktop"; their setters throw otherwise), renderScale works wherever the game runs, clipboard works on Windows, macOS, Linux and the web (and in headless runs and tests, which have an in-memory clipboard), not on phones and tablets. An unknown name throws with a "did you mean". borderless needs a desktop window (Windows, macOS, Linux; not the web), monitors needs a desktop window that can list and move between monitors (Windows, macOS, Linux; true with one monitor too: offer the choice when window.monitors().length > 1). Read window.supports("frameCap") before offering window.frameCap.

items.name: ClipboardAPI
items.doc: The clipboard. A game with a window reads and writes the system clipboard on Windows, macOS, Linux and the web; headless runs and tests have an in-memory one (it starts empty in every test); phones and tablets have none yet: window.supports("clipboard") is false there and read() rejects with code "unsupported". A focused TextField already pastes with Ctrl+V (Cmd+V) and copies with Ctrl+C (Cmd+C), without any script.

members.doc: Resolves with the text on the clipboard ("" when it holds none or something that is not text). On the web the browser lets a page read the clipboard only inside a paste, so it resolves with the text of the last paste (the player pressed Ctrl+V or Cmd+V in the page). Rejects with code "unsupported" where there is no clipboard (phones, tablets). In a replay the text a read returned is recorded and given back, so a paste replays the same. Example: const text = await clipboard.read();

Puts `text` on the clipboard. Throws when it is not a string. Does nothing where there is no clipboard. The web lets a page write only during a key press or click, so a write made in the middle of a frame may not reach the browser's clipboard. Example: clipboard.write("ABC123");

items.name: CaptureTextureOptions
items.doc: What render.captureTexture takes.

members.doc: Width of the texture in pixels, a whole number from 1 to 2048.
Height of the texture in pixels, a whole number from 1 to 2048.

What to do when width : height is not the frame's aspect ratio. "cover" (default) cuts the middle part with that ratio out of the frame, so nothing is distorted and the long side loses its edges; "stretch" squeezes the whole frame into the size.

items.name: Texture
items.doc: A picture made at run time (render.captureTexture, render.textureFromPNG). Put `id` in a texture field, for example entity.get("Sprite").texture = tex.id, or a Panel's texture or a Button's icon, like the path of an asset; a Sprite with no `size` takes the texture's pixel size. It lives until destroy() (or the end of the game): the engine keeps at most 32 at a time, so destroy the ones you stop showing. Stop showing a texture (destroy its entity or change its texture field) before you destroy it: a frame that still names it draws the missing-texture checker and logs why. The pixels are also kept in memory (width x height x 4 bytes) so toPNG() works in every run. Example: const tex = render.captureTexture({ width: 256, height: 144 }); storage.set("slot1.png", tex.toPNG()); entity.get("Sprite").texture = tex.id;

members.doc: What a texture field takes in place of an asset path ("runtime:3"). Numbers count from 1 in each run and are never reused.
Width in pixels.
Height in pixels.

True when the run has no renderer (a headless run without graphics): the picture is a flat colour of the size asked, not a capture. A normal run, a headless run with graphics and every test with a GPU give false.
True after destroy().

The picture as a PNG file, Base64 encoded (a string, because storage keeps JSON): storage.set("slot1.png", tex.toPNG()). render.textureFromPNG takes it back. A 256 x 144 picture of a town is about 20 to 60 KB of text; storage.set(key, value, { compress: true }) shrinks it a little. Throws after destroy().
Frees the texture's memory. Safe to call twice. Do not keep showing it afterwards.

items.name: RenderAPI
items.doc: Pictures of the running game as textures, for a save slot, a photo mode or a minimap snapshot (docs/SCRIPTING.md, "Render"). A texture's pixels are those of a screenshot of the same frame.

members.doc: Makes a texture of the picture the player sees: the last frame that was drawn, with the HUD and every camera, at the size asked (the frame is read back from the GPU on Metal, OpenGL, Direct3D 11 and WebGL2, then resampled on the CPU). Called from a script during a frame it gives the frame before it; in a test it draws the current state first, like game.screenshot, and with the same size as the game target (game.screenSize, times window.renderScale) its pixels are exactly the screenshot's. In a run without a renderer (graphics off) it gives a flat placeholder of the size asked (texture.placeholder is true) so the code that saves and shows it still runs. Throws for a size outside 1 to 2048 and when 32 textures are alive. Example: const tex = render.captureTexture({ width: 256, height: 144 });

A texture from the text texture.toPNG() returned (Base64 of a PNG file; a data:image/png;base64,... URL works too), at most 2048 x 2048. Throws a teaching Error for text that is not a PNG or JPG/BMP/TGA image, and when 32 textures are alive. Synchronous: no Promise, so there is nothing to check afterwards. Example: const pic = storage.get("slot1.png", null); if (pic) entity.get("Sprite").texture = render.textureFromPNG(pic).id;

items.name: MeshMaterialOptions
items.doc: The look of one submesh of a procedural mesh: the fields of a glTF material the renderer reads. Pass a plain string instead of an object to give only the name.

members.doc: What MeshRenderer.materialColors is keyed by to recolor this submesh (materialColors: { skin: [1, 0.5, 0.4, 1] }), and the material name in a saved .glb. Default "".
Base color factor: a color(), an [r, g, b, a] array or "#rrggbb". Multiplied with MeshRenderer.color. Default white.
Base color texture: a project image path, or a Texture from render.captureTexture (shown, but mesh.save refuses a run-time texture because the file would point to nothing). Default none.
0 to 1. With roughness, replaces MeshRenderer.metallic and roughness for this submesh. Default 0 once either is given.
0 to 1. Default 0.6 once either metallic or roughness is given.
Light the surface gives off (rgb), added after lighting. Default black.
Draw the back faces too (a leaf, a flag). Default false: only counter-clockwise triangles are drawn.
Alpha-blended with the color's alpha and the texture's; drawn far to near with the other transparent meshes. Default false.

items.name: MeshSubmeshOptions
items.doc: A run of the index list drawn with one material. Submeshes of one mesh share its vertices and are drawn in order.

members.doc: The submesh's material (a name, or the object). Default: an unnamed white material.
First index of the run, a multiple of 3 (indices, not triangles). Default: where the previous submesh ends (0 for the first).
Number of indices, a multiple of 3 and at least 3. Default: up to the end of the index list.

items.name: MeshOptions
items.doc: What mesh.create and mesh.update take. Arrays may be plain arrays or typed arrays (a Float32Array is read without copying through the language); numbers may be flat or grouped, [x, y, z, x, y, z] or [[x, y, z], [x, y, z]] or [{x, y, z}]. Coordinates are glTF's: +Y up, right-handed, counter-clockwise triangles face front, uv (0, 0) is the top-left of the image (v grows downwards).

members.doc: Three numbers per vertex. Required in create; kept when left out of update. At most 1048576 vertices.

Vertex numbers, three per triangle. In create, left out = every three vertices make a triangle (0,1,2 then 3,4,5...). In update, left out = kept. At most 6291456 indices. Every entry must be a vertex of positions.

Three numbers per vertex, normalized for you. Left out = computed: smooth, weighted by triangle area, averaging the triangles that share a vertex (duplicate the vertices of a hard edge). Normals are never kept from an earlier call: pass them again with every update, or let them be computed.
Two numbers per vertex. Left out = zeros in create, kept in update.

members.doc: Validates the arrays and makes a mesh. Missing normals and tangents are computed. Throws a teaching Error naming the field and the entry for a wrong array length, an index outside the vertices, a submesh outside the index list, NaN, or when 256 meshes are alive. Example: const m = mesh.create({ positions: [0,0,0, 1,0,0, 0,1,0], indices: [0, 1, 2], submeshes: [{ material: { name: "skin", color: "#e0b090" } }] }); entity.get("MeshRenderer").mesh = m.id;

members.sig: update(mesh: Mesh | string, options: MeshOptions): Mesh
members.doc: Replaces what `options` gives and keeps the rest; cheap enough to call every frame: the GPU buffers are reused while the new data fits (a second change of the same mesh within one frame makes new ones). Bounds follow, so culling and picking stay right; a Collider3D that uses the mesh rebuilds its shape on every update (a mesh collider on a mesh deformed each frame is expensive: update it less often, or use a primitive collider). Throws for a destroyed or unknown mesh, or when the new arrays do not fit together. Returns the Mesh when given one.
Frees the mesh. Entities that still name it draw a placeholder box and the engine logs why once; set their mesh first. Throws for an unknown id, not for a Mesh that was destroyed already.

It loads back as a normal asset: MeshRenderer.mesh = path. A material whose texture is a run-time texture cannot be saved (throws). A mesh without metallic or roughness is saved with the defaults (0 and 0.6).
True while the mesh is alive in the current scene.
The live meshes of the current scene.

items.name: StorageAPI
items.doc: Persistent JSON save data, one file per key in <user dir>/storage/ (an older storage.json is split into them at the first start). Tests and `--storage memory` runs use a throw-away in-memory object instead.

members.sig: get<T = any>(key: string, fallback?: T): T
set(key: string, value: Json, options?: { compress?: boolean }): void
members.doc: Stores `value` under `key` and writes that key's file now (atomically: temporary file, then rename), so a save costs the size of its own key only. `{compress: true}` stores the value zlib-compressed (smaller on disk, for big saves; storage.get returns the same value either way). The write blocks the frame; use setAsync for a big value. Throws on an empty key or an unknown option.

members.sig: setAsync(key: string, value: Json, options?: { compress?: boolean }): Promise<number>
members.doc: Like set, but the file is encoded (and compressed when asked) and written off the frame: on a worker thread on desktop and mobile, between frames on the web (no threads there). storage.get returns the new value at once; the Promise resolves with the file's size in bytes when the file is written, and rejects with the reason if it could not be. Writes to one key land in the order they were asked, and a later set, remove, clear or size waits for the pending ones. Serializing `value` into JSON still happens in this call.
Bytes the key's file takes (the compressed size for a compressed value); 0 when the key is not stored. Waits for pending setAsync writes.
The keys of the game's own values. The engine's own ("factoria.analytics", "factoria.remoteConfig") are not listed.
Removes every value, the engine's too: the player is asked about analytics again.

True when a storage file (a key's file in storage/, or an older storage.json) did not parse at the first use of storage in this run (a crash or a bad edit damaged it). The engine kept the damaged file as storage.corrupt.json in the save folder (storage.corrupt.2.json, .3... if one is already there; it never replaces one) and the game started without that file's data (the other keys load), so nothing is lost for good: a script can tell the player ("your save was damaged") or offer a recovery. Writes are atomic (temporary file, then rename), so a crash during a save leaves the previous file intact. False when the file was fine or missing, in memory runs and in tests (unless game.setStorageText gave a damaged text).

items.name: RngAPI
items.doc: Deterministic random numbers (seeded per run). Math.random is routed here too.

members.doc: Inclusive.

Reseeds the deterministic world RNG (use from tools/tests for seed -> level determinism). The running game draws from this one RNG, so reseeding it changes the game's random sequence: a level generator should use rng.create(seed) instead.

Creates an independent, deterministic generator with the same methods as rng. It has its own state and never reads or changes the world RNG (or Math.random), so a tool can generate a level from a seed without disturbing the running game. Algorithm: mulberry32 (32-bit state, one step per draw). The algorithm and the draws each method consumes are STABLE across engine versions, so a stored seed keeps giving the same sequence. The seed is reduced to 32 bits (ToUint32: integer part, modulo 2^32); 0 is a valid seed. Throws for a non-number or non-finite seed. Example: const r = rng.create(7); r.int(1, 6).

items.name: Rng
items.doc: An independent seeded generator from rng.create(seed). Algorithm mulberry32, stable across engine versions: the same seed gives the same sequence on every platform. Every method draws a fixed number of 32-bit steps (float, range, int and chance: one per call; pick: one, none for an empty array; shuffle: items.length - 1), so a sequence does not depend on the arguments.

members.doc: Next number in [0, 1): a 32-bit step divided by 2^32.
min + (max - min) * float(); in [min, max).
Integer in [min, max], both inclusive (arguments are truncated to integers): min + floor(float() * (max - min + 1)). Returns min when max <= min (still one draw).
True with probability p (default 0.5): float() < p.
A random item (items[floor(float() * length)]), or undefined for an empty array.
A shuffled copy (Fisher-Yates from the end, j = floor(float() * (i + 1))); the input is not modified.

The generator's 32-bit state, an integer from 0 to 4294967295: one number that is the whole stream. Store it in a save and assign it later (or create the generator with it as the seed: rng.create(state) continues exactly where state was read) to resume the sequence. STABLE across engine versions like the algorithm. Assigning anything that is not such an integer throws. Example: const saved = r.state; r.float(); r.state = saved; r.float() // the same number again.
Restarts this generator from seed n (same reduction as rng.create); the same as a new rng.create(n). Does not touch the world RNG.
